body:
A content workflow review checks how an idea becomes a published piece and whether the process reliably produces useful, accurate work. Start with a few recent examples rather than buying another tool or redesigning the whole process. A shared document can be enough to record findings, owners and next actions.

## 1. Follow a small sample from brief to publication

Select a mix of recent posts, emails or articles, including one that needed substantial rework. For each, collect the original brief, source material, first draft, reviewer comments and final version. Record who handled each stage and where work waited or returned for another revision.

Agree what good work should achieve: answer a customer question, explain an offer or help a reader take an informed next step. Likes alone cannot establish whether the content was useful or accurate.

- Does the brief identify the audience, purpose, format and intended next step?
- Can the writer find the approved facts, product details and examples?
- Are drafting, editing, factual review and final approval assigned to someone?
- Is there one clearly identifiable current version?

## 2. Check usefulness before polishing the wording

Compare the draft with the promise in its title or opening line. A guide should explain how to do the task; a product post should make the offer and its limits understandable. Remove filler that does not help the reader decide or act.

Ask whether the piece offers a concrete example, a useful explanation or a practical step. Check that the format suits its destination: a newsletter needs context, while a short social post may need one focused point. Repurposed pieces should adapt the explanation rather than repeat identical text everywhere.

Google's [people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) provides useful questions about originality, completeness and whether the reader leaves with a satisfying answer. Apply those questions to the content itself, not as a requirement to add length.

## 3. Verify facts and brand consistency separately

Use a short list of claims to verify against current, reliable evidence. Check names, dates, prices, calculations, quotations, product availability and any promised results. Follow source links and confirm that they support the actual statement. AI-generated wording is not evidence.

- Mark unsupported claims for removal, qualification or further checking.
- Label invented examples as illustrative; never present them as customer results.
- Confirm permission before including client details, testimonials or confidential material.
- Check the offer against what the business currently provides.

Then review voice and terminology. Compare the draft with an approved example: is it appropriately direct, formal or conversational? Use consistent product names and avoid claims that exaggerate capability. Keep the factual meaning intact when adjusting tone.

## 4. Make editing and approval distinct steps

The editor improves structure, clarity, spelling and accessibility. A factual reviewer checks claims and limitations. For sensitive or regulated topics, involve an appropriately qualified reviewer. A small business may assign several roles to one person, but each check should still happen.

Agree who gives final approval and where that decision is recorded. Identify the approved version, date and intended channel. If a price, claim or offer changes afterwards, send the affected material back for review rather than assuming the earlier approval still applies.

Before publication, open the final links, check the call to action and inspect the preview on a phone. Review captions, image descriptions and any text embedded in visuals. Make sure the final asset matches the approved copy.

## 5. Look for recurring workflow problems

**Repeated tone corrections:** The brief says only 'make it professional'. Add one approved example and specific voice preferences, then check whether the next draft needs fewer corrections.

**Conflicting product claims:** Writers use an old pricing document. Identify one maintained source of product facts and an owner who confirms updates before they are reused.

**Approval delays:** Several people assume someone else is reviewing. Name the final approver and agree when comments are due, without treating silence as approval.

**Repetition across channels:** One caption is copied into every format. Give each version a clear purpose, then use the [repurposing quality-control checklist](/blog/content-repurposing-quality-control-checklist) to review the outputs together.

**A correction appears in only one version:** Keep related assets under one brief reference and record where each was used. Check all affected versions when an important fact changes.

## 6. Make one improvement and review the result

Choose the recurring issue causing the most avoidable rework or factual risk. Record the change, owner and next review date. For the next small batch, compare revision rounds, time waiting for approval and corrections needed after publication. Record context so a more complex assignment is not mistaken for a worse process.

ContentOS can help prepare and refine drafts in the [Studio](/studio). Factual checking, approval and publication decisions remain with your business; the checklist below is a human review process, not an automated approval feature.

## Reusable quality-review checklist

- The audience, purpose, channel and next step are clear.
- The title and opening accurately describe what the content delivers.
- The draft provides useful detail without filler or unnecessary repetition.
- Facts, figures, quotations, links and current product claims are checked.
- Examples are accurate or clearly labelled illustrative.
- Sensitive information and permissions have been reviewed.
- Brand voice, names and terminology match the approved reference.
- Editing and factual checks are complete.
- A named approver has approved the final version.
- Links, mobile presentation and visual text have been checked.
- Related versions reflect any material corrections.
- Recurring problems have an owner and a follow-up date.
